notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: Bollards have double orange reflectors on the front and a single white one on the back; rarer blue and red variants exist.

notes.subject: guardrail
notes.text: A wider-than-normal type B guardrail, used by no other European country except its eastern neighbour.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Wide round concrete poles, often in pairs, with short metal bars holding the insulators.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Some pole tops have two support bars forming an inverted triangle, others a trident with two upward arms; the trident is unique to this country and its neighbour.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Striped gas and water poles, like snow poles, often stand beside the road.

notes.subject: street
notes.text: Lamp posts have thick bases fixed by opposing pairs of bolts, and temporary red-and-white striped square sign posts are common.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Chevrons are white with red arrows, less often red on yellow.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Hiking markers show one coloured stripe between two white ones, sometimes forming an arrow; bicycle versions use yellow stripes.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Arrow-shaped direction signs have a filled tip and can be recognised from behind; the eastern neighbour uses small white arrows.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Road sign borders are separated from the edge by a strip in the sign's background colour.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Street signs are mostly bright red, wide on walls or thin on posts; blue ones are also common; the word ulice is sometimes shown.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: House numbers are on blue or red signs with thin white borders.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Sign posts usually have thick black caps.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Pedestrian signs show five stripes at a larger scale than in the eastern neighbour.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Road signs use a fairly thin font; the eastern neighbour's is much bolder.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Kilometre markers have a yellow outline outside the black frame and no black middle line.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Black signs at the end of bridges show the road number on the left in generation 4 coverage.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: A Slavic language with acute accents plus Ř, Ě and Ů; the word for street is ulice rather than ulica.

notes.subject: line
notes.text: Often solid outer lines with no centre line, also common in the northwest neighbour.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Rolling countryside with many hills but few tall mountains.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Well-kept prefab panel apartment blocks, often with vibrant colours and patterns; diamond-shaped roof tiles are common too.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Suburban houses are commonly joined in pairs.

notes.subject: car
notes.text: Much generation 3 was shot in winter, so it looks grey and sometimes snowy; antennas often have grey tape.

notes.subject: car
notes.text: Red, black and white generation 4 cars exist, and a rare generation 2; the eastern neighbour has no white car or generation 2.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Railway crossing signs have no background.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Road numbers start with 1 to 6; roads 7, 8 and 9 all start in the capital and head north and northwest.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: About 95 percent of wine comes from the southeast, in Moravia.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: The north has rolling land with steep solitary hills, sometimes crowned by castles.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Timber-framed houses are mostly along the northern border with the northwest neighbour; dark wooden upper floors on thick poles occur in the far north.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Moravian town houses sit long side to the road, joined in groups, with barn-sized front doors, as in northeast of its southern neighbour.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Highly decorated folk baroque village houses surround České Budějovice.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Blue street signs are more common in the east; Ostrava mainly uses them.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: A white street sign with blue text and a red border means you are near the eastern border.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Four-digit bike path numbers increase clockwise from South Bohemia; paths starting with A are only in the capital.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Downtown streets of the capital are paved with grey and white marble, like Portugal.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Cube-shaped functionalist red brick houses in Zlín were built for shoe factory workers.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Brno has pairs of black and white house numbers, with the district on the black one.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Plzeň house numbers are two octagonal red and white plates with inverted colours.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Red house numbers with a dividing line and a Roman numeral are unique to Liberec.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Písek uses yellow house numbers with a black outline.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Bilingual street signs with Polish appear in Český Těšín.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Šumperk street signs are blue with text filling nearly the whole sign.
